title: Ang 1353–1360: Salok Sehskriti
hook: Guru Nanak's and Guru Arjan's verses in an old literary style
tomorrow: small poems where every verse ends on the same word. what word?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jaijavanti, the last raga: four hymns of the ninth Guru, and two loving ways to sing them. Today the ragas are over.

A friend at a job interview switches voices: more formal, bigger words, a straighter back. She isn't faking. She's speaking the room's language. Right after the last raga, on ang 1353, the Granth switches voices too. These saloks are called Sehskriti, and the sound changes: heavier, older, close to the learned speech of the pandits. Guru Nanak and Guru Arjan both wrote in it. So why borrow the pandits' style?
screen: `THE INTERVIEW VOICE.` → `THE GRANTH SWITCHES VOICES.` → `WHY THE PANDITS' STYLE?`

segments.voice: Say a line aloud, even in transliteration, and you feel it in your mouth: clustered consonants, endings that ring like temple Sanskrit. Scholars describe it as a literary style that borrows Sanskrit's sound without being classical Sanskrit. Now hear what Guru Nanak says in it. In paraphrase, his first salok here walks through a learned man's day. He reads the books and says the evening prayers. He argues, worships stones, sits in trance like a heron. He wears the beads and the forehead mark. And then: if he knew the One, he'd know all of this, by itself, is empty. So the challenge arrives in the challenger's own accent. A pandit can't wave it off as rough village talk; it sounds like his own books. That's the move: speak the room's language, then say what the room needs to hear. Guru Arjan's saloks in the same style run on longer, and the weight of the sound carries their theme: a world that passes, and the Name that holds. No grammar is needed to feel it. These are words made to be heard. The old style is an old key, turned in an old lock.
screen: `A STYLE WITH SANSKRIT'S SOUND.` · `BOOKS, PRAYERS, BEADS, MARKS.` · `EMPTY WITHOUT THE ONE.` · `THE ROOM'S OWN ACCENT.` · then, large: `THE OLD STYLE.`

segments.voice: Hum one low note and feel where it lands: your chest, your throat, the bones of your face. Let it fade, and sit in the quiet it leaves, the way a heavy line keeps ringing after it's said. Hum again whenever you like.
Ang 1353. Where Salok Sehskriti begins, in an old learned style, and Guru Nanak uses it to say learning without the One is empty.
For the road: the old style, because sometimes a true thing lands best in the listener's own accent. That's today.

howItsDone: Salok Sehskriti is read in the Granth's closing pages after the ragas, and readers often say its lines aloud slowly, since the style's sound is part of its weight.

fork.setup: your uncle only listens to arguments in formal, scholarly English. you want to tell him something true about kindness. what does Salok Sehskriti suggest?
options: say it in his register, carefully, so the true thing can land.
use your plainest slang; style never changes whether a point lands.
don't bother; the Gurus only spoke to farmers, never to scholars.
fork.reveal: Guru Nanak spoke to the learned in a style close to their own, and used it to say that learning without the One is empty. the style served the point.
